summary: Describes a mechanism for advertising IPv6 prefixes in BGP that are tied to Color Extended Communities, to build end-to-end intent-aware paths for SRv6 services. These Colored Prefixes are the SRv6 locators, and the mechanism is called Colored Prefix Routing.

plainLanguage.summary: Roads can get colors that mean fast, cheap or safe. This lets the network advertise addresses with colors so traffic takes the kind of road it needs.

questions: how does colored prefix routing work
subtitle: Advertises IPv6 prefixes with colors in BGP to establish intent-aware paths for SRv6 services across domains.

tldr.problem: When SRv6 services span multiple autonomous systems, there is a need to establish end-to-end paths that meet different service intents (low latency, high bandwidth, etc.) without requiring new BGP extensions or complex label swapping at domain boundaries.
tldr.mechanism: Colored Prefix Routing (CPR) advertises IPv6 prefixes associated with Color Extended Communities in BGP. SRv6 locators are split into sub-locators (Colored Prefixes) for different intents. Service SIDs under these locators are routed using longest prefix matching, automatically steering traffic through intent-aware paths.
tldr.outcome: SRv6 services are steered to appropriate inter-domain paths based on color-matching without transport-layer encapsulation overhead, leveraging existing BGP IPv6 and Color Extended Community mechanisms for easy interoperability and incremental deployment.

today: RFC 9723 is an Informational RFC published in May 2025 by the IETF community. It describes an operational methodology for inter-domain intent-aware routing in SRv6 and hybrid networks, leveraging existing standards for easy deployment in multi-AS environments.

sections.title: Intent-Aware Routing Across Domains
sections.content:
Modern networks carry many different services with different requirements. A video service might need low latency, a bulk backup service needs high bandwidth, and a financial transaction needs high reliability. As services cross autonomous system (AS) boundaries, the need arises to provide different end-to-end paths based on service intent.

Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) provides a foundation for this by allowing services to be assigned with Service Segment Identifiers (SIDs) under different SRv6 locator prefixes. This document describes Colored Prefix Routing (CPR), which associates SRv6 locators with color values representing intents. Colors are carried in the existing Color Extended Community mechanism in BGP, allowing services to be steered to appropriate paths without requiring new BGP extensions or complex inter-domain label swapping.
sections.plainLanguage: When traffic crosses from one network to another, it might need special treatment. This gives each road a color and advertises which roads are available, so packets automatically take the right-colored road for their needs.

sections.title: Colored Prefix Concept and Allocation
sections.content:
Colored Prefixes are IPv6 prefixes associated with a specific intent via a color value in the Color Extended Community. In SRv6 networks, Colored Prefixes are SRv6 locators or sub-locators (smaller address blocks carved from a base locator) that correspond to different intents.

For example, if a Provider Edge (PE) node is allocated the base SRv6 locator 2001:db8:aaaa:1::/64 and needs to support 16 different intents, this base locator is split into 16 sub-locators from 2001:db8:aaaa:1:0000::/68 to 2001:db8:aaaa:1:f000::/68. Each sub-locator is a Colored Prefix associated with a different intent such as low-delay, high-bandwidth, or high-reliability. SRv6 service SIDs allocated under these colored locators inherit the intent of their parent locator.
sections.plainLanguage: An address block is divided into colored parts, each meaning a different kind of service. Services get addresses from the right colored part so the network knows what kind of treatment they need.

sections.title: Advertisement and Path Resolution
sections.content:
Provider Edge nodes originate BGP IPv6 unicast routes for their Colored Prefixes, carrying the Color Extended Community that indicates the intent. These routes are advertised across domain boundaries with hop-by-hop next-hop updates at each border router, just like standard BGP IPv6 routes.

When a domain receives a Colored Prefix route, border nodes can resolve it to an intra-domain color-aware path using the tuple (next-hop, color). This intra-domain path can be built using any existing mechanism such as SRv6 Policy, SR-MPLS Policy, SRv6 Flex-Algo, SR-MPLS Flex-Algo, or RSVP-TE. At borders between AS boundaries, the color value is typically preserved (allowing consistent color-to-intent mapping throughout trusted domains), but color translation is possible where different domains use different color values for the same intent.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network broadcasts which colored roads it has available to reach PE nodes. When traffic arrives at a border, the network checks the color and picks the right internal road to get there.

sections.title: Service Routing and Forwarding
sections.content:
SRv6 services are assigned Service SIDs under Colored Prefixes, embedding the intent in the SID itself. For example, an SRv6 VPN service with low-delay intent is allocated the SID PE3:CL1:DT6::, where PE3:CL1:: is the low-delay Colored Prefix. The service route is advertised using standard SRv6 mechanisms without carrying a Color Extended Community.

When an ingress PE receives a service route, it forwards packets destined for that service by using the Service SID as the destination address in an outer IPv6 header. If a Colored Prefix route matching the service's locator prefix has been received, the network performs longest prefix matching to find an intra-domain color-aware path. This process repeats at each domain boundary, creating an end-to-end path that respects the service intent without requiring any transport-layer label or SID, resulting in smaller encapsulation overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Services get addresses that say what color they are. When a packet travels, at each network border the system finds the right colored road to continue on.

sections.title: Deployment and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
CPR is designed for deployment within trusted domains—a single operator's networks or multiple operators with established operational trust. The mechanism reuses existing IPv6 Address Family and Color Extended Community, enabling interoperability with legacy systems and incremental deployment.

To ensure Colored Prefixes reach all relevant ingress PEs and border nodes, route aggregation must be disabled for IPv6 unicast routes carrying the Color Extended Community. Each Colored Prefix should be associated with one intent; multiple copies with different colors are considered misconfiguration.

In mixed environments where some intermediate AS use MPLS instead of SRv6, CPR routes can still be advertised using the IPv6 unicast address family. Border nodes use route resolution policies to map CPR routes to intra-domain MPLS LSPs. For legacy domains that do not support CPR, border nodes can ignore the color and resolve the route over a best-effort path, allowing CPR deployment to be incremental and backward-compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: This works inside a trusted group of networks. If a network does not understand colors, it just ignores them and sends traffic the normal way. This makes it possible to deploy colors slowly without breaking anything.
